newsitem.title: USA: Fed says economy growing steadily, prices muted.
newsitem.headline: Fed says economy growing steadily, prices muted.

text.p: The economy ploughed ahead in February with scant sign of runaway wages or prices, the Federal Reserve said Wednesday, even though there were shortages of skilled employees across the country.
Coming just two weeks before central bank policy makers meet to consider whether to raise interest rates for the first time in more than two years, the report was broadly reassuring about inflation.
"Tight labour markets still dominate in almost all parts of the country," said the Fed's Beige Book summary, so named for the colour of its cover.
"Nevertheless, wage gains remain generally moderate," it added. "Price pressures, such as those reported by most retail and manufacturing contacts, appear to have been temperate."
Policy makers will use the report when they gather March 25. The Beige Book reports are issued eight times a year. The last one was issued Jan. 22.
On the basis of interviews before March 3 with in all 12 Fed districts, the central bank concluded the economy had continued to grow "at a relatively moderate pace."
The Fed said wage gains seemed to be stuck in a 3 percent to 4 percent range, but there were "pockets of persistently upward wage gains" in speciality areas like computer software.
It also said businesses across the country said they were having difficulty finding and keeping new employees because of tight labour markets.
"Shortages of engineers and construction, skilled manufacturing and high-tech workers are most often noted," the Fed said.

Analysts said the report seemed to signal inflation pressures near the surface, but not yet bubbling through in the form of threatening wage and price hikes that would push the Fed to raise interest rates March 25.

"There's no smoking gun here," said economist Paul Kasriel of Northern Trust Co. in Chicago. "There seems to be a lot of strength in economic activity across the country, but it's not manifesting itself in the form of higher prices."

The Fed said price increases at retailers and manufacturers were generally temperate, partly because stiff competition made it hard to boost prices. Some Fed districts said rising productivity was offsetting higher costs for wages and raw materials.

Manufacturing activity was reported continuing at a generally high level and, in some cases, was growing. The Fed said there were only pockets of weakness, principally in industries like apparel where production was going overseas, and in paper and textile industries.
Kasriel said "pre-conditions for higher prices were developing," noting some firms said they couldn't expand output any more because of labour shortages.

Nonetheless, he said odds were that the Fed will keep rates steady at its March 25 meeting, in part out of concern that raising them would draw policital criticism that the action was being taken to dampen stock market prices.
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan warned earlier this month that stock prices may be too high.

"He (Greenspan) got such a negative response to his stock market comments that I think the political risks have tipped against a tightening (in March)," Kasriel said, shifting the likelihood more toward the following meeting in May.
Retail sales were higher during February than a year ago in most districts, with strong business for cosmetics, building materials, pharmaceuticals and home furnishings.
"Current inventories are generally at or slightly below desired levels," the Fed said, noting some reports of short supplies of popular new vehicles.

Demand for all types of loans, whether from consumers or real estate and commercial borrowers, was described as "decidedly mixed," though more Fed districts said loans were steady or falling than reported them on the rise.
Consumer loan requests, for example, were increasing at a slower rate in the Chicago Fed district, but demand was mixed or flat in Atlanta and Cleveland.
"There appears to be no consistent trend in consumer loan quality," the Fed said, with delinquencies on the rise in the Cleveland and New York Fed districts but improving in Atlanta and Philadelphia.
